prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you type an address like https://example.com/products into a browser, nothing has been sent yet, and the browser's first job is to understand what you typed. It parses the string into a scheme (https), a host (example.com), an optional port (443 by default for HTTPS), a path, and any query string or fragment. It also checks a few local rules before touching the network. If the host is on the browser's HSTS preload list, or the site previously sent a Strict-Transport-Security header, the browser will refuse to use plain HTTP at all. It also looks in its own caches, because a fresh cached copy of the resource, or an existing open connection to the same origin, lets it skip many of the steps that follow.

The browser cannot connect to a name, only to an IP address, so the next step is DNS resolution. The browser checks its own DNS cache first, then asks the operating system, which checks its cache and the hosts file. If neither knows the answer, the request goes to a recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP or a public provider. That resolver does the real work if it has no cached answer. It asks a root server which servers handle the .com top-level domain, asks one of those which servers are authoritative for example.com, and finally asks an authoritative server for the A record (an IPv4 address) and often the AAAA record (an IPv6 address). Each answer carries a time-to-live telling caches how long they may reuse it. This is why a freshly changed DNS record can take a while to reach everyone, and why the first visit to a site is slower than repeat visits. Many sites also have several addresses, or use DNS to steer you to a nearby data centre or CDN edge server, so two people resolving the same name can get different answers.

With an IP address in hand, the browser opens a TCP connection to port 443. TCP provides an ordered, reliable stream of bytes on top of unreliable packet delivery, and it begins with a three-step handshake. The client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client answers with an ACK. This costs one full round trip, meaning the time for a packet to reach the server and for the reply to return. Round-trip time is dominated by physical distance and network congestion, which is why geography matters so much for latency and why CDNs exist. Modern browsers may also race IPv4 and IPv6 connection attempts, a technique called Happy Eyeballs, and use whichever answers first. If the site supports HTTP/3, the story is different, because that protocol runs over QUIC on UDP and merges the transport and encryption handshakes, but the logical steps are much the same.

Because the address says https, the connection must be encrypted and authenticated before any HTTP is sent. This is done with TLS. In the TLS 1.3 handshake, the client opens with a ClientHello that lists the protocol versions and cipher suites it supports, a random value, and a key share for key exchange. Crucially it also includes the Server Name Indication extension, which carries the hostname in the clear so that a server hosting many sites on one IP address knows which certificate to present. It may also list the application protocols it can speak, such as h2 for HTTP/2 and http/1.1, through ALPN. The server picks a cipher suite, sends its own key share, and from the two shares both sides independently compute the same shared secret without it ever crossing the wire. Everything after that point is encrypted. The server then sends its certificate chain and a signature proving it holds the matching private key, followed by a Finished message.

The certificate is how the browser decides whether this server is genuinely example.com and not an impostor. The browser walks the chain from the server's certificate through any intermediates up to a root certificate authority that is already trusted by the operating system or browser. It verifies each signature, confirms the certificate has not expired, and checks that the hostname appears in the certificate's subject alternative names. It may also check revocation status, though in practice this is often handled through short-lived certificates or stapled OCSP responses sent by the server. If any check fails, the browser shows the familiar full-page warning rather than proceeding, which is the browser protecting you from a man-in-the-middle. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for this exchange, and with session resumption a returning client can sometimes send encrypted data immediately, saving even that.

Now, finally, the browser can speak HTTP. It builds a request containing a method, here GET, the path /products, and a set of headers. These include Host, which names the site, along with Accept and Accept-Encoding, User-Agent, and any cookies the browser has stored for this domain. If the connection negotiated HTTP/2, these are packed into binary frames with compressed headers, and the browser may reuse this single connection for many requests in parallel. With HTTP/1.1 the same information is sent as readable text lines. Either way, the request travels through the encrypted tunnel, split into TCP segments and then IP packets, and hops across routers between you and the server.

Often the machine that receives the request is not the application itself. It may be a CDN edge node, a load balancer, or a reverse proxy such as nginx, which terminates TLS, may answer straight from its cache, and otherwise forwards the request to an application server. That server routes the path to some handler, which may read a database, render a template, or call other services before producing a response. The server then sends back a status line and headers, such as 200 OK and a Content-Type, followed by the body. The moment the first byte of that response reaches the browser is called time to first byte, or TTFB. It is a useful metric because it adds up nearly everything described here: DNS lookup, the TCP handshake, the TLS handshake, the network transit of the request, and the server's own processing time before it starts replying.

For a junior developer, the practical lesson is that a lot happens before your code runs, and most of it is waiting on round trips. That is why reusing connections, enabling HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, serving content from locations near users, caching aggressively, and keeping server-side work fast all reduce the delay before the first byte, and why the browser's network panel breaks a request into separate timing phases for exactly these stages.
